texts.0: SP, due to an incomplete altimeter cross-check during level-off, did not arrest the vertical rate at the assigned altitude and did not re-establish level flight. The altitude deviation exceeded 300 ft and was still developing when the IP intervened on the controls to return the aircraft to the assigned altitude. SP did not identify the divergence until it was called.
texts.1: SP, due to a delayed pitch and power correction after entering the climb, allowed altitude to diverge to approximately 300 ft, at the limit of the standard. SP corrected only after repeated verbal prompting by the IP, and the return to the assigned altitude was slow. Altitude was eventually regained without IP intervention on the controls.
texts.2: SP, due to a coarse pitch input at level-off, overshot the assigned altitude by about 200 ft, between the 150 ft and 300 ft limits. SP detected the deviation on the altimeter and vertical speed indicator and corrected it in good time, without prompting and without IP intervention. The following level flight segment was held closer to the assigned altitude.
texts.3: SP maintained altitude within 150 ft in climb, descent, level-off, level flight and turns up to 30 degrees of bank. Corrections were prompt and were made with smooth pitch and power inputs. Deviations were detected early on the altimeter and never developed further.
texts.4: SP held the assigned altitude with negligible deviation throughout all phases of flight, including level-offs from climb and descent and turns up to 30 degrees of bank. Pitch and power were adjusted before any measurable divergence appeared. Altitude control required no comment or correction from the IP at any point.
texts.marginal: SP kept altitude within standards, but the deviations clustered near the outer part of the acceptable band, mainly at level-off from the climb. The trend was a repeated overshoot that SP corrected each time rather than anticipated. SP is expected to lead the level-off earlier so that the assigned altitude is captured with a tighter margin.

texts_at.1: SP corrected altitude only after repeated verbal prompting from the IP, with the divergence reaching approximately 300 ft, at the limit of the standard, because the pitch and power correction after entering the climb had been delayed. The slow return to the assigned altitude followed once the prompting had been given. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to begin the correction on the VSI trend without needing it prompted.
texts_at.2: SP detected an overshoot of about 200 ft on the altimeter and vertical speed indicator and corrected it in good time without prompting, after a coarse pitch input at level-off had produced the excursion, between the 150 ft and 300 ft limits. The following level flight segment was held closer to the assigned altitude. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to size the level-off pitch input more finely so the overshoot does not develop.
texts_at.3: SP maintained altitude within 150 ft in climb, descent, level-off, level flight and turns up to 30 degrees of bank, with corrections prompt and made through smooth pitch and power inputs as soon as a deviation was detected on the altimeter. The deviations clustered toward the outer part of the band at level-off from the climb. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to lead the level-off earlier so the deviations settle nearer the target.

texts_above.2: SP detected an altitude overshoot of about 200 ft on the altimeter and vertical speed indicator, between the 150 ft and 300 ft limits, correcting it in good time without prompting after a coarse pitch input at level-off produced the excursion. The following level segment was held closer to the assigned altitude. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good altitude control on the level-off.
texts_above.3: SP maintained altitude within 150 ft in climb, descent, level-off, level flight and turns up to 30 degrees of bank on every segment, with corrections prompt and smooth and every deviation detected early on the altimeter. No level-off on the sortie needed a secondary correction. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate altitude control on the level-off.
texts_above.4: SP held the assigned altitude with negligible deviation throughout every phase of flight, including level-offs from climb and descent and turns up to 30 degrees of bank, adjusting pitch and power before any measurable divergence appeared. Altitude control drew no comment from the IP at any point. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent altitude control on the level-off.

texts.0: SP, due to power settings not matched to the phase of flight, allowed airspeed to diverge by more than 20 KIAS from the target and did not recognize the divergence. The deviation was still increasing when the IP took the controls and reset power to recover the target airspeed. SP did not include the airspeed indicator in the scan during the transition.
texts.1: SP, due to a late power reduction at level-off, allowed airspeed to build to about 20 KIAS above the target, at the limit of the standard. SP reduced power only after the IP called the airspeed, and the recovery to the target was slow. No IP input on the controls was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a power change made in one coarse step, allowed airspeed to deviate by roughly 15 KIAS from the target, between the 10 and 20 KIAS limits. SP identified the trend on the airspeed indicator and restored the target speed in good time without prompting. Subsequent power changes were made in smaller increments.
texts.3: SP maintained airspeed within 10 KIAS of the target in climb, descent, level flight and turns up to 30 degrees of bank. Power was set for the phase of flight as determined by the Flight Manual, and small deviations were trapped early. Airspeed control did not degrade while altitude and heading corrections were being flown.
texts.4: SP held the target airspeed with negligible deviation through every phase of flight, including power and configuration changes. Power was anticipated and set before any speed trend developed. Airspeed remained stable even while SP flew simultaneous altitude and heading corrections.
texts.marginal: SP kept airspeed within standards, but the values sat consistently on the fast side of the target during descents. The trend was a reactive rather than anticipated power reduction, which left little margin before the limit. SP is expected to set descent power earlier so that airspeed stabilizes closer to the target.

texts_at.1: SP reduced power only after the IP called the airspeed, with the buildup reaching about 20 KIAS above target, at the limit of the standard, because the power reduction at level-off had come late. The recovery to the target airspeed was slow once the call had been given. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to reduce power on the level-off pitch change without needing the airspeed called.
texts_at.2: SP identified an airspeed trend of roughly 15 KIAS on the indicator and restored the target speed in good time without prompting, after a power change made in one coarse step had produced the deviation, between the 10 and 20 KIAS limits. texts_at.3: SP maintained airspeed within 10 KIAS of the target in climb, descent, level flight and turns up to 30 degrees of bank, with power set for the phase of flight and small deviations trapped early. One power change trailed the phase transition by a moment before the trend was caught. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to set power at the moment of the phase change rather than a moment after it.

texts_above.2: SP identified an airspeed trend of roughly 15 KIAS on the indicator, between the 10 and 20 KIAS limits, restoring the target speed in good time without prompting after a power change made in one coarse step produced the deviation. Later power changes were made in smaller increments. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound airspeed control across phase changes.
texts_above.3: SP maintained airspeed within 10 KIAS of the target in climb, descent, level flight and turns up to 30 degrees of bank on the whole sortie, with power set for the phase of flight as determined by the Flight Manual and small deviations trapped early. Airspeed control did not degrade while other corrections were being flown. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed airspeed control across phase changes.
texts_above.4: SP held the target airspeed with negligible deviation through every phase of flight, including power and configuration changes, anticipating power and setting it before any speed trend developed even while flying simultaneous altitude and heading corrections. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior airspeed control across phase changes.

error_modes.label: Heading control and roll-out accuracy (+/- 5 deg / +/- 10 deg)

texts.0: SP, due to roll-out inputs made without reference to the HSI, stopped the turn more than 10 degrees from the assigned heading and continued to drift away from it. SP did not re-establish the assigned heading and the IP intervened to stop the divergence. The heading error was not identified by SP at any stage.
texts.1: SP, due to a rate of turn that was not reduced before the roll-out, stopped the turn about 10 degrees from the assigned heading, at the limit of the standard. SP corrected only after the IP called the heading, and the correction was applied late. The assigned heading was re-established without IP control input.
texts.2: SP, due to a late start of the roll-out from a 30 degree bank turn, overshot the assigned heading by roughly 8 degrees, between the 5 and 10 degree limits. SP recognized the overshoot on the HSI and returned to the assigned heading promptly and without prompting. Later turns were rolled out with an appropriate lead.
texts.3: SP maintained heading within 5 degrees in level flight and rolled out of turns up to 30 degrees of bank on the assigned heading. Turns were coordinated and the roll-out lead was correctly judged. Small heading errors were seen on the HSI and removed immediately.
texts.4: SP held assigned headings with negligible error throughout, including turns up to 30 degrees of bank flown while altitude and airspeed corrections were in progress. The roll-out lead was consistently accurate and needed no secondary correction. Heading control was maintained without any comment from the IP.
texts.marginal: SP kept heading within standards, but the errors were repeatedly close to the outer edge of the band after turns in one direction. The trend was a consistent slight overshoot corrected after the roll-out rather than prevented by lead. SP is expected to refine the roll-out lead so that headings are captured without a follow-up correction.

texts_at.1: SP re-established the assigned heading only after the IP called it, having stopped the turn about 10 degrees from the assigned heading, at the limit of the standard, because the rate of turn had not been reduced before the roll-out. The same drift reappeared before the next roll-out heading before the call was given. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to reduce the rate of turn ahead of the roll-out without needing the heading called.
texts_at.2: SP recognized an overshoot of roughly 8 degrees on the HSI and returned to the assigned heading promptly and without prompting, after a late start to the roll-out from a bank angle of 30 degrees had let the aircraft pass the heading, between the 5 and 10 degree limits. Later turns were rolled out with an appropriate lead. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to start the roll-out lead earlier so the overshoot does not develop.
texts_at.3: SP maintained heading within 5 degrees in level flight and rolled out of turns up to 30 degrees of bank on the assigned heading, with turns coordinated and the roll-out lead judged correctly and small errors removed immediately from the HSI. One roll-out was judged a touch tighter than the others needed. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to judge every roll-out lead as precisely as the best one.

texts_above.2: SP recognized an overshoot of roughly 8 degrees on the HSI, between the 5 and 10 degree limits, returning to the assigned heading promptly without prompting after a late start to the roll-out from a bank angle of 30 degrees let the aircraft pass the heading. Later turns were rolled out with an appropriate lead. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady heading and roll-out accuracy.
texts_above.3: SP maintained heading within 5 degrees in level flight and rolled out of every turn up to 30 degrees of bank on the assigned heading, with turns coordinated and the roll-out lead judged correctly on each occasion and small errors removed immediately. No roll-out on the sortie needed a follow-up correction. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise heading and roll-out accuracy.
texts_above.4: SP held assigned headings with negligible error throughout, including turns up to 30 degrees of bank flown while altitude and airspeed corrections were in progress, with the roll-out lead consistently accurate and needing no secondary correction. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to first-rate heading and roll-out accuracy.

texts.0: SP, due to an interrupted instrument cross-check that fixed attention on a single indicator, did not monitor aircraft state during the transition between phases of flight. Altitude, airspeed and heading diverged simultaneously beyond the standards and SP did not detect the trend. The IP intervened on the controls to restore the flight parameters.
texts.1: SP, due to an absent cross-check of aircraft state against the primary flight instruments while re-setting a cockpit control, allowed two parameters to reach the outer limits of the standards at the same time. SP restored the scan only after the IP called the deviations, and the recovery was slow. No IP control input was needed.
texts.2: SP, due to a scan that dwelt too long on the attitude indicator, was late in noticing developing altitude and airspeed trends at level-off. The deviations reached the mid-range of the acceptable band before SP restored a full cross-check and corrected them in good time. No prompting or IP intervention was required.
texts.3: SP maintained a continuous cross-check of the primary flight instruments through climb, descent, level-off, level flight and turns. Deviations in altitude, airspeed and heading were detected while still small and were corrected within the tight standards. The scan was not interrupted by secondary cockpit tasks.
texts.4: SP sustained a complete and evenly paced instrument cross-check in every phase of flight, including while managing switches and radios. Trends were identified before they became measurable deviations, so the corrections needed were minimal. The scan remained intact under increased task load.
texts.marginal: SP maintained an adequate cross-check overall, but the scan narrowed noticeably whenever a correction to one parameter was in progress. The trend was that a second parameter began to drift on each occasion, although always within standards. SP is expected to keep the full scan running while corrections are being flown.

texts_at.1: SP had the deviations called by the IP before the scan was restored, with two parameters having reached the outer limits of the standards, because the cross-check of aircraft state had gone missing while a cockpit control was being reset. The scan slowed briefly during one secondary cockpit task before returning to rate. The standard for the Training Section was met. Neither trend was allowed to develop further. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid instrument cross-check through phase transitions.
texts_above.3: SP maintained a continuous cross-check of the primary flight instruments through climb, descent, level-off, level flight and turns on the whole sortie, detecting every deviation in altitude, airspeed and heading while still small and holding it within the tight standards. The scan was not interrupted by secondary cockpit tasks at any point. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate instrument cross-check through phase transitions.
texts_above.4: SP sustained a complete and evenly paced instrument cross-check in every phase of flight, including while managing switches and radios, identifying trends before they became measurable deviations so the corrections needed were minimal. The scan remained intact under increased task load throughout. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary instrument cross-check through phase transitions.

error_modes.label: Engine power management for the phase of flight

texts.0: SP, due to power settings not selected for the phase of flight as determined by the Flight Manual, did not control the engine power so as to hold the flight parameters. Airspeed and altitude departed the standards together and the aircraft was left in an undesired energy state, requiring IP intervention. SP did not associate the parameter deviations with the power setting.
texts.1: SP, due to power changes made only after the flight parameters had already moved, held altitude and airspeed at the limits of the standards. SP set the correct power only after verbal guidance from the IP at each phase change. Engine limits were respected and no IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP, due to power selected in coarse steps rather than set and then refined, produced parameter excursions in the middle of the acceptable band at the climb and descent entries. SP recognized that the power setting was the cause and adjusted it in good time without prompting. The remaining transitions were flown with smaller power adjustments.
texts.3: SP controlled engine power appropriately for each phase of flight, as determined by the Flight Manual and as required to maintain altitude, airspeed and heading. Power was set at the start of each transition rather than in response to a deviation. Engine handling was smooth and within all limits.
texts.4: SP anticipated the power requirement for every phase of flight and set it precisely, so that the flight parameters were held with negligible deviation. Power changes were smooth, correctly timed and coordinated with pitch and trim. No re-adjustment was needed after any transition.
texts.marginal: SP managed engine power within standards, but the settings were arrived at by trial adjustment rather than selected directly. The trend was a small parameter excursion at every phase change before the power settled. SP is expected to select the known power setting for each phase so the parameters are held from the outset.

texts_at.1: SP had the correct power setting called by the IP at each phase change, holding altitude and airspeed at the limits of the standards, because power changes had been made only after the flight parameters had already moved. Engine limits were respected once the setting had been called. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to set power at the phase change itself without needing it called each time.
texts_at.2: SP recognized that the power setting was the cause of a parameter excursion in the middle of the acceptable band at the climb and descent entries, and adjusted it in good time without prompting, after power selected in coarse steps rather than set and refined had produced the excursion. The remaining transitions were flown with smaller power adjustments. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to set power directly at each entry rather than in coarse steps.
texts_at.3: SP controlled engine power appropriately for each phase of flight, as determined by the Flight Manual and as required to maintain altitude, airspeed and heading, with power set at the start of each transition rather than in response to a deviation. One transition needed a small refinement to the initial setting. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to set the final power value in one movement on the next sortie.

texts_above.2: SP recognized that the power setting was the cause of a parameter excursion in the middle of the acceptable band at a climb entry, and adjusted it in good time without prompting after power selected in coarse steps had produced the excursion. The remaining transitions were flown with smaller adjustments. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable engine power management for the phase of flight.
texts_above.3: SP controlled engine power appropriately for every phase of flight, as determined by the Flight Manual and as required to maintain altitude, airspeed and heading, with power set at the start of each transition rather than in response to a deviation. Engine handling stayed smooth and within all limits throughout. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good engine power management for the phase of flight.
texts_above.4: SP anticipated the power requirement for every phase of flight and set it precisely, so the flight parameters were held with negligible deviation, with power changes smooth, correctly timed and coordinated with pitch and trim and no re-adjustment needed after any transition. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior engine power management for the phase of flight.

error_modes.label: Trim technique across the airspeed range

texts.0: SP, due to a skill-based error in trim technique, did not handle the aileron, elevator and rudder trim correctly across the airspeed range. The aircraft was flown with large out-of-trim control forces, the parameters exceeded the standards, and the IP intervened to re-trim and stabilize the aircraft. SP did not recognize that the out-of-trim condition was driving the deviations.
texts.1: SP, due to trim applied only after the control forces had become large, worked against sustained out-of-trim pressures during the airspeed changes. Parameters were held at the limits of the standards and SP re-trimmed only after being prompted by the IP. Control of the aircraft was retained without IP control input.
texts.2: SP, due to elevator trim run in large steps after each speed change, was left with residual control pressures that produced mid-band altitude excursions. SP recognized the out-of-trim condition and refined the trim in good time without prompting. The later speed changes were trimmed progressively as the speed stabilized.
texts.3: SP handled aileron, elevator and rudder trim correctly and with ease throughout the airspeed range and in all maneuvers. The aircraft was kept in trim during and after each speed and power change, so the parameters were held within the tight standards with light control forces.
texts.4: SP trimmed the aircraft continuously and precisely in all three axes, keeping control forces effectively at zero across the full airspeed range. Trim was run during the speed change rather than after it, so no parameter excursion appeared. Aircraft handling was comfortable and unhurried throughout.
texts.marginal: SP trimmed adequately and remained within standards, but rudder trim was routinely left unattended after power changes. The trend was a small residual yaw that SP compensated with foot pressure instead of trim. SP is expected to include rudder trim in the standard sequence after every power change.

texts_at.1: SP re-trimmed only after being prompted by the IP, holding the parameters at the limits of the standards while working against sustained out-of-trim pressures during the airspeed changes, because trim had been applied only after the control forces had become large. Control of the aircraft was retained once the prompting had been given. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to trim as the control force builds rather than after it has become large.
texts_at.2: SP recognized an out-of-trim condition and refined the trim in good time without prompting, after elevator trim run in large steps had left residual pressures that produced mid-band altitude excursions. Later speed changes were trimmed progressively as the speed stabilized. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to run the elevator trim in smaller steps so the residual pressure does not appear.
texts_at.3: SP handled aileron, elevator and rudder trim correctly and with ease throughout the airspeed range and in all maneuvers, keeping the aircraft in trim during and after each speed and power change so the parameters were held within the tight standards with light control forces. Rudder trim was left a moment after one power change before being applied. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to include rudder trim in the same movement as every power change.

texts_above.2: SP recognized an out-of-trim condition and refined the trim in good time without prompting, after elevator trim run in large steps left a residual pressure that produced a mid-band altitude excursion. Later speed changes were trimmed progressively as the speed stabilized. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured trim technique across the airspeed range.
texts_above.3: SP handled aileron, elevator and rudder trim correctly and with ease throughout the airspeed range and in every maneuver, keeping the aircraft in trim during and after each speed and power change so the parameters were held within the tight standards with light control forces. Rudder trim was included in every power change without exception. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed trim technique across the airspeed range.
texts_above.4: SP trimmed the aircraft continuously and precisely in all three axes, keeping control forces effectively at zero across the full airspeed range, running trim during the speed change rather than after it so no parameter excursion ever appeared. Aircraft handling stayed comfortable and unhurried throughout. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional trim technique across the airspeed range.

error_modes.label: Radio aids, orientation and recovery to departure or alternate

texts.0: SP, due to a loss of situational awareness in the working area, was not cognizant of the operation of the available radio aids and could not use them to maintain orientation. SP was unable to state a heading to the departure or the alternate airport and the IP took over the navigation to recover the aircraft. Aircraft control also degraded beyond the standards while SP tried to interpret the navigation display.
texts.1: SP, due to incomplete set-up of the navigation aids before the maneuvers, lost track of the position relative to the departure airfield. SP re-established orientation only after step-by-step verbal guidance from the IP on which aid to select and how to read it. The flight parameters were held at the limits of the standards while this was done.
texts.2: SP, due to attention concentrated on aircraft control, was late in checking the radio aids and briefly lost the bearing to the alternate airport. SP recovered orientation without prompting by returning to the navigation display in good time, with the parameters staying in the mid-range of the standards. The route back to the departure airfield was then flown correctly.
texts.3: SP was cognizant of the operation of the available radio aids and used them to maintain orientation throughout. SP identified the position relative to the departure and alternate airfields on request and flew accurate headings towards them on flight instruments and radio aids, holding altitude, airspeed and heading within the tight standards.
texts.4: SP maintained a continuous and accurate picture of position from the radio aids without any interruption to aircraft control. SP could state the bearing to the departure and alternate airfields at any moment and turn towards either immediately. Navigation and instrument flying were handled together with no loss of precision.
texts.marginal: SP used the radio aids correctly and kept orientation, but the position picture was rebuilt on request rather than maintained continuously. The trend was a short pause in aircraft control each time SP interrogated the navigation display. SP is expected to update orientation in small steps within the normal scan.

texts_at.1: SP re-established orientation only after step-by-step verbal guidance from the IP on which aid to select and how to read it, with the flight parameters held at the limits of the standards while this was done, because the navigation aids had not been fully set up before the maneuvers. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to complete the navigation aid set-up before the maneuvers start.
texts_at.2: SP recovered orientation without prompting by returning to the navigation display in good time, with the parameters staying in the mid-range of the standards, after attention concentrated on aircraft control had let the bearing to the alternate airport be briefly lost. The route back to the departure airfield was then flown correctly. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to check the radio aids on a schedule rather than only when aircraft control allows.
texts_at.3: SP was cognizant of the operation of the available radio aids and used them to maintain orientation throughout, identifying the position relative to the departure and alternate airfields on request and flying accurate headings toward them while holding altitude, airspeed and heading within the tight standards. One interrogation of the display took a moment longer than the others. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to read every aid as quickly as the fastest one.

texts_above.2: SP recovered orientation without prompting by returning to the navigation display in good time, with the parameters staying in the mid-range of the standards, after attention on aircraft control had briefly let the bearing to the alternate airport go unchecked. The route back to the departure airfield was then flown correctly. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to competent use of radio aids for orientation.
texts_above.3: SP was cognizant of the operation of the available radio aids and used them to maintain orientation throughout the sortie, identifying the position relative to the departure and alternate airfields on request and flying accurate headings toward them while holding altitude, airspeed and heading within the tight standards. No interrogation of the display cost a lapse in aircraft control. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to disciplined use of radio aids for orientation.
texts_above.4: SP maintained a continuous and accurate picture of position from the radio aids without any interruption to aircraft control, able to state the bearing to the departure and alternate airfields at any moment and turn toward either immediately, with navigation and instrument flying handled together with no loss of precision. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to faultless use of radio aids for orientation.

error_modes.label: Aircraft handling comfort and switch operation

texts.0: SP, due to unfamiliarity with the cockpit layout, did not handle the aircraft with comfort and ease and did not use the switches flawlessly, selecting the wrong control on more than one occasion. Control inputs were abrupt and out of phase with the aircraft response, and the resulting deviations exceeded the standards. The IP intervened to restore the correct configuration and stabilize the aircraft.
texts.1: SP, due to slow and hesitant switch selections that required prolonged head-down time, flew jerky corrections and held the parameters at the limits of the standards. SP completed the selections correctly only after verbal direction from the IP. No IP control input was required.
texts.2: SP, due to over-controlling in pitch and roll while searching for switches, produced deviations in the middle of the acceptable band. SP recognized the coarse handling, softened the inputs and completed the switch selections correctly in good time and without prompting. Handling improved noticeably over the remainder of the sortie.
texts.3: SP handled the aircraft with comfort and ease and used the aircraft switches flawlessly. Control inputs were smooth and proportionate, and switch selections were made without interrupting aircraft control or exceeding the tight standards.
texts.4: SP flew the aircraft with evident comfort and ease, using inputs that were smooth, small and correctly timed. Switch selections were made accurately and almost without looking, with no effect at all on the flight parameters. Cockpit handling was well above the standard expected at this stage.
texts.marginal: SP handled the aircraft and its switches to standard, but the inputs were firmer than necessary and every switch selection drew the eyes into the cockpit. The trend was a small parameter wobble accompanying each selection, always within limits. SP is expected to smooth the control inputs and learn the switch positions well enough to select them by feel.

texts_at.1: SP completed the switch selections only after verbal direction from the IP, flying jerky corrections and holding the parameters at the limits of the standards, because slow and hesitant selections had required prolonged head-down time. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to select the correct switch directly without needing the direction given.
texts_at.2: SP recognized coarse handling produced by over-controlling in pitch and roll while searching for switches, softened the inputs and completed the switch selections correctly in good time and without prompting, with the resulting deviations in the middle of the acceptable band. Handling improved noticeably over the remainder of the sortie. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to soften the control inputs before the search for the switch begins, not after.
texts_at.3: SP handled the aircraft with comfort and ease and used the aircraft switches flawlessly, with control inputs smooth and proportionate and switch selections made without interrupting aircraft control or exceeding the tight standards. One selection needed a slightly longer look than the others. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to find every switch as quickly as the fastest one.

texts_above.2: SP recognized coarse handling produced by over-controlling in pitch and roll while searching for a switch, softened the inputs and completed the selection correctly in good time and without prompting, with the resulting deviation in the middle of the acceptable band. Handling improved for the rest of the sortie. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady aircraft handling and switch operation.
texts_above.3: SP handled the aircraft with comfort and ease and used the aircraft switches flawlessly on every selection, with control inputs smooth and proportionate and no switch selection interrupting aircraft control or exceeding the tight standards. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate aircraft handling and switch operation.
texts_above.4: SP flew the aircraft with evident comfort and ease, using inputs that were smooth, small and correctly timed, with switch selections made accurately and almost without looking and no effect at all on the flight parameters, well above the standard expected at this stage. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent aircraft handling and switch operation.

error_modes.label: Level off lead point (10 percent of VSI) and half-pitch technique

texts.0: SP, due to starting the level off with no lead point taken from the vertical speed, did not begin the pitch change until the assigned altitude was already at the altimeter and never cut the pitch in half. The aircraft went through the altitude by more than 300 ft with the vertical rate still high, and the IP intervened on the controls to capture it. SP did not recognize the overshoot until it was called.
texts.1: SP, due to a lead point far smaller than 10 percent of the indicated vertical speed, began the level off late and made the whole pitch change in one movement. The overshoot reached about 300 ft, at the limit of the standard, and was corrected only after repeated IP prompting. No IP input on the controls was required.
texts.2: SP, due to using a fixed lead point instead of 10 percent of the indicated vertical speed, was late levelling off from a high rate climb and overshot by roughly 200 ft, between the 150 ft and 300 ft limits. SP saw the trend on the VSI and altimeter and recovered the assigned altitude in good time without prompting. The following level off was led correctly.
texts.3: SP took the lead point as 10 percent of the indicated vertical speed, cut the pitch in half at that point and then continued the pitch change smoothly to level flight. The assigned altitude was captured within 150 ft, power was adjusted approaching the target airspeed and the aircraft was trimmed. Level offs from climb and from descent were flown to the same standard.
texts.4: SP led every level off with 10 percent of the indicated vertical speed and halved the pitch at the lead point, so the assigned altitude was captured with negligible deviation. Power was set for the target airspeed as the nose reached level flight and trim followed immediately. The transitions drew no comment from the IP.
texts.marginal: SP used a lead point taken from the vertical speed and stayed within standards, but the pitch change was made in one movement instead of being halved first. The trend was an abrupt capture with the altitude settling from above on each level off. SP is expected to cut the pitch in half at the lead point so the level off is smooth.

texts_at.1: SP had the correction corrected only after repeated IP prompting, with the overshoot reaching about 300 ft, at the limit of the standard, because the lead point had been chosen without reference to the rate of climb for a climb of about 2000 feet per minute. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to convert the vertical speed into a lead point without needing it prompted.
texts_at.2: SP recognized a developing overshoot from a fixed lead point applied regardless of rate of climb, lowered the nose and returned to the restriction altitude promptly without IP input, holding it to roughly 200 ft, between the 150 ft and 300 ft limits, then set power for the desired airspeed and trimmed. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to scale the lead point to the actual rate rather than use a fixed value.
texts_at.3: SP used a lead point of approximately 10 percent of the VSI at each published altitude restriction and smoothly lowered the nose to level flight at that point, adjusting the PCL to the desired airspeed and trimming, with each restriction captured within 150 ft and no overshoot. One level-off used a lead point a touch smaller than the rate called for. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to apply the 10 percent relationship consistently on every restriction.

texts_above.2: SP recognized a developing overshoot from a lead point that had not been scaled to a higher rate of climb, lowering the nose and returning to the restriction altitude promptly without IP input at about 200 ft, between the 150 ft and 300 ft limits, then setting power and trim. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good level-off lead-point technique.
texts_above.3: SP used a lead point of approximately 10 percent of the indicated vertical speed at every published altitude restriction, capturing each one within 150 ft with power adjusted to the desired airspeed and the aircraft trimmed as the level-off was completed. No restriction on the sortie needed a secondary correction. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed level-off lead-point technique.
texts_above.4: SP led every level-off with 10 percent of the indicated vertical speed and halved the pitch at the lead point, so the assigned altitude was captured with negligible deviation and power was set for the target airspeed as the nose reached level flight with trim following immediately. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional level-off lead-point technique.

error_modes.label: Known pitch and power settings and continual power changes

texts.0: SP, due to not starting from the known pitch and power settings, set torque by trial and error and made continual power changes throughout. The heading, pitch and trim disturbances that followed drove altitude beyond 300 ft and heading beyond 10 degrees and kept diverging until the IP took the controls and set a known value. SP could not state the torque required for the phase of flight.
texts.1: SP, due to chasing the performance instruments instead of setting a known pitch attitude and torque, needed repeated large power corrections to hold the parameters. Altitude and heading were driven to about 300 ft and 10 degrees, at the limits of the standards, and settled only after the IP called out the torque to set. Control of the aircraft was retained without IP control input.
texts.2: SP, due to setting an approximate torque and then correcting it in several successive steps, produced pitch and trim changes that moved altitude by roughly 200 ft, between the 150 ft and 300 ft limits. SP recognized that the power was being chased, returned to the known setting for that phase of flight and stabilized the parameters in good time without prompting.
texts.3: SP started from the known pitch and power settings for each manoeuvre and adjusted only slightly for fuel load and density altitude. Power changes were few and small, so heading, pitch and trim stayed steady and the parameters were held within 150 ft, 10 KIAS and 5 degrees. The EADI and torque were used as control instruments and the altimeter, airspeed indicator, VSI and heading were crosschecked as performance instruments.
texts.4: SP set the known pitch attitude and torque for each phase of flight before any parameter could move and needed almost no further power change. Altitude, airspeed and heading remained effectively on target, with no trim or heading disturbance traceable to power handling. SP stated the expected torque for each manoeuvre in advance.
texts.marginal: SP worked from known pitch and power settings and stayed within standards, but each setting was reached through two or three successive torque corrections. The trend was a small pitch and heading disturbance with every power change, always inside the limits. SP is expected to select the known torque in one movement and let the parameters settle before correcting.

texts_at.1: SP had the torque called out by the IP before the parameters settled, with altitude and heading having reached about 300 ft and 10 degrees, at the limits of the standards, because the performance instruments had been chased instead of a known pitch attitude and torque being set. Control of the aircraft was retained once the torque had been called. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to set the known torque directly without needing it called.
texts_at.2: SP recognized that power was being chased, returned to the known setting for that phase of flight and stabilized the parameters in good time without prompting, after setting an approximate torque and correcting it in several successive steps had moved altitude by roughly 200 ft, between the 150 ft and 300 ft limits. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to select the known setting in one movement rather than approach it in steps.
texts_at.3: SP started from the known pitch and power settings for each maneuver and adjusted only slightly for fuel load and density altitude, so power changes were few and small and heading, pitch and trim stayed steady, with the EADI and torque used as control instruments and altimeter, airspeed indicator, VSI and heading crosschecked as performance instruments. One setting was reached through two small corrections rather than one. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to reach every known setting in a single movement.

texts_above.2: SP recognized that power was being chased and returned to the known setting for the phase of flight, stabilizing the parameters in good time without prompting after an approximate torque correction had moved altitude by roughly 200 ft, between the 150 ft and 300 ft limits. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid use of known pitch and power settings.
texts_above.3: SP started from the known pitch and power settings for every maneuver and adjusted only slightly for fuel load and density altitude, so power changes stayed few and small and heading, pitch and trim held steady within 150 ft, 10 KIAS and 5 degrees throughout the sortie. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate use of known pitch and power settings.
texts_above.4: SP set the known pitch attitude and torque for each phase of flight before any parameter could move and needed almost no further power change, with altitude, airspeed and heading remaining effectively on target and no trim or heading disturbance traceable to power handling. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary use of known pitch and power settings.

error_modes.label: Composite crosscheck balance and over-reliance on instrumentation

texts.0: SP, due to over-reliance on instrumentation to maintain aircraft attitude, accumulated excessive head-down time and did not establish the attitude by positioning the nose and wings in relation to the horizon. Fixation on a single cue let altitude and heading run beyond 300 ft and 10 degrees before the IP intervened on the controls. Clearing for other aircraft was effectively abandoned.
texts.1: SP, due to a crosscheck weighted almost entirely to the flight instruments although the horizon was clearly discernable, held attitude by reacting to indications rather than by outside references. Deviations reached about 300 ft and 10 degrees, at the limits of the standards, and were corrected only after IP prompting to look outside and clear. No IP control input was needed.
texts.2: SP, due to concentrating on one cue instead of cycling check, correct and check the next parameter, slowed the crosscheck and let altitude drift roughly 200 ft, between the 150 ft and 300 ft limits. SP recognized the fixation, went back to the outside attitude picture crosschecked with the instruments and recovered in good time without prompting.
texts.3: SP flew composite, setting and holding attitude with the nose and wings referenced to the horizon and devoting about 80 percent of the crosscheck to outside references and clearing and 20 percent to the flight instruments. Small attitude changes not visible outside were trapped on the instruments, so the parameters stayed within 150 ft, 10 KIAS and 5 degrees. Trim was used to remove control pressures at each new attitude.
texts.4: SP kept the composite crosscheck moving without interruption, checking one parameter, correcting it and moving to the next, with attitude always set against the horizon and confirmed on the instruments. Deviations were negligible and clearing for other aircraft was continuous. Head-down time never grew enough to affect lookout or aircraft control.
texts.marginal: SP flew composite within standards, but head-down time grew noticeably whenever a correction was needed. The trend was a pause in clearing each time SP went inside to confirm the attitude. SP is expected to set the attitude on the horizon first and use the flight instruments only to confirm it.

texts_at.1: SP had corrected only after IP prompting to look outside and clear, with deviations reaching about 300 ft and 10 degrees, at the limits of the standards, because attitude had been held by reacting to instrument indications rather than by outside references although the horizon was clearly discernable. No IP control input was needed. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to reference the horizon first without needing the prompt to look outside.
texts_at.2: SP recognized a fixation on one cue, returned to the outside attitude picture crosschecked with the instruments and recovered in good time without prompting, after concentrating on one cue instead of cycling check, correct and check the next parameter had let altitude drift roughly 200 ft, between the 150 ft and 300 ft limits. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to keep the cycle moving so no single cue is held that long.
texts_at.3: SP flew composite, setting and holding attitude with the nose and wings referenced to the horizon and devoting about 80 percent of the crosscheck to outside references and clearing and 20 percent to the flight instruments, trapping small attitude changes on the instruments so the parameters stayed within 150 ft, 10 KIAS and 5 degrees. Clearing paused briefly during one correction. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to keep clearing active through every correction, not just most of them.

texts_above.2: SP recognized a fixation on one cue and returned to the outside attitude picture crosschecked with the instruments, recovering in good time without prompting after concentrating on one cue had let altitude drift roughly 200 ft, between the 150 ft and 300 ft limits. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good composite crosscheck balance.
texts_above.3: SP flew composite on the whole sortie, setting and holding attitude with the nose and wings referenced to the horizon and devoting about 80 percent of the crosscheck to outside references and clearing and 20 percent to the flight instruments, holding the parameters within 150 ft, 10 KIAS and 5 degrees throughout. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding composite crosscheck balance.

error_modes.label: Pitch compensation for loss of vertical lift in the turn
error_modes.source: technique:7.8 TURNS AND TURNS TO HEADINGS

texts.0: SP, due to not increasing pitch attitude to counteract the loss of vertical lift whenever the aircraft was banked, let the nose fall through in every turn. Altitude loss went beyond 300 ft and the vertical rate was still increasing when the IP intervened on the controls to recover level flight. SP did not connect the altitude loss with the bank.
texts.1: SP, due to backpressure applied only after the VSI already showed a descent, lost about 300 ft in the turns, at the limit of the standard. The nose was raised only after repeated IP prompting and the altitude was regained slowly. SP kept control of the aircraft without IP input on the controls.
texts.2: SP, due to backpressure that lagged the bank as the angle increased, allowed a descent of roughly 200 ft in the turn, between the 150 ft and 300 ft limits. SP detected the nose-low attitude on the VSI, reduced the bank slightly, adjusted backpressure and regained the altitude in good time without prompting. The remaining turns were flown level.
texts.3: SP increased the pitch attitude as the bank was established, so the loss of vertical lift was compensated as it occurred and altitude was held within 150 ft in turns up to 30 degrees of bank. The VSI was crosschecked to detect nose-low or nose-high trends, and a small power increase held the airspeed.
texts.4: SP applied backpressure simultaneously with the bank in every turn, so no vertical rate developed at entry, in the established turn or during the rollout. Altitude remained effectively constant and airspeed was held by a power addition made at the same moment. Turn entries and rollouts were flown without any parameter excursion.
texts.marginal: SP held altitude within standards in the turns, but the aircraft settled slightly low before the backpressure went in. The trend was a reactive rather than simultaneous pitch input as the bank increased. SP is expected to raise the nose as the bank goes on rather than after the VSI moves.

texts_at.1: SP had the nose raised only after repeated IP prompting, having lost about 300 ft in the turns, at the limit of the standard, because backpressure had been applied only after the VSI already showed a descent. Altitude was regained slowly once the prompting had been given. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to apply backpressure with the bank rather than after the VSI moves.
texts_at.2: SP detected a nose-low attitude on the VSI, reduced the bank slightly, adjusted backpressure and regained the altitude in good time without prompting, after backpressure lagging the bank had let a descent of roughly 200 ft develop, between the 150 ft and 300 ft limits. The remaining turns were flown level. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to apply backpressure as the bank goes on rather than after the VSI shows the descent.
texts_at.3: SP increased the pitch attitude as the bank was established, compensating the loss of vertical lift as it occurred and holding altitude within 150 ft in turns up to 30 degrees of bank, crosschecking the VSI for nose-low or nose-high trends with a small power increase holding the airspeed. One turn settled a touch low before the correction caught it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to bring every turn entry to the same timing as the best one.

texts_above.2: SP detected a nose-low attitude on the VSI and reduced the bank slightly to regain the altitude in good time without prompting, after backpressure lagging the bank had let a descent of roughly 200 ft develop, between the 150 ft and 300 ft limits. The remaining turns were flown level. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady pitch compensation for the loss of vertical lift.
texts_above.3: SP increased the pitch attitude as the bank was established on every turn, compensating the loss of vertical lift as it occurred and holding altitude within 150 ft in turns up to 30 degrees of bank with a small power increase holding the airspeed. No turn on the sortie needed the altitude recovered after the fact. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed pitch compensation for the loss of vertical lift.
texts_above.4: SP applied backpressure simultaneously with the bank in every turn, so no vertical rate developed at entry, in the established turn or during the rollout, with altitude remaining effectively constant and airspeed held by a power addition made at the same moment. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent pitch compensation for the loss of vertical lift.

error_modes.label: Smooth and even control pressure versus abrupt inputs

texts.0: SP, due to rough and erratic use of the controls, applied rapid and abrupt inputs to which the aircraft reacted accordingly, alternating between excessive backpressure and insufficient backpressure. Altitude swung beyond 300 ft and airspeed beyond 20 KIAS without settling, and the IP took the controls to steady the aircraft. SP did not soften the inputs when the oscillation was called.
texts.1: SP, due to control pressure applied in abrupt steps instead of smoothly and evenly, drove the aircraft into repeated climbs and descents of about 300 ft, at the limit of the standard. The inputs were moderated only after repeated IP prompting and the parameters settled slowly. No IP intervention on the controls was required.
texts.2: SP, due to a rapid control input at the start of a correction, overshot by roughly 200 ft in altitude, between the 150 ft and 300 ft limits, with a matching airspeed excursion. SP recognized that the input had been abrupt, changed to smooth and even pressure and stabilized the parameters in good time without prompting.
texts.3: SP applied control pressure smoothly and evenly and orchestrated aileron, elevator and rudder together, so corrections were completed without overshoot. Aircraft control was a continuous succession of minor corrections and the parameters were held within 150 ft, 10 KIAS and 5 degrees.
texts.4: SP flew with almost imperceptible corrections and applied every control pressure smoothly, so no aircraft reaction to a rough input appeared at any point. The three controls were used as a single coordinated input. The parameters remained effectively on target throughout the sortie.
texts.marginal: SP kept the parameters within standards, but the corrections were made with firmer and larger inputs than the deviation called for. The trend was a small overshoot after each correction which SP then had to take out. SP is expected to apply control pressure smoothly and evenly and to correct in smaller increments.

texts_at.1: SP had the inputs moderated only after repeated IP prompting, driving the aircraft into repeated climbs and descents of about 300 ft, at the limit of the standard, because control pressure had been applied in abrupt steps instead of smoothly and evenly. The parameters settled slowly once the prompting had been given. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to apply pressure smoothly from the first input without needing it moderated.
texts_at.2: SP recognized that an input had been abrupt, changed to smooth and even pressure and stabilized the parameters in good time without prompting, after a rapid control input at the start of a correction had produced an overshoot of roughly 200 ft in altitude with a matching airspeed excursion, between the 150 ft and 300 ft limits and the 10 and 20 KIAS limits. This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to size the first input smoothly so no correction is needed afterward.
texts_at.3: SP applied control pressure smoothly and evenly and orchestrated aileron, elevator and rudder together, so corrections were completed without overshoot and aircraft control stayed a continuous succession of minor corrections holding the parameters within 150 ft, 10 KIAS and 5 degrees. One correction was a shade firmer than the others needed. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to bring every correction to the same lightness as the smoothest one.

The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable smooth and even control inputs.
texts_above.3: SP applied control pressure smoothly and evenly and orchestrated aileron, elevator and rudder together on every correction, so corrections completed without overshoot and aircraft control stayed a continuous succession of minor corrections holding the parameters within 150 ft, 10 KIAS and 5 degrees. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise smooth and even control inputs.
texts_above.4: SP flew with almost imperceptible corrections and applied every control pressure smoothly, so no aircraft reaction to a rough input appeared at any point, using the three controls as a single coordinated input with the parameters remaining effectively on target throughout the sortie. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional smooth and even control inputs.

error_modes.label: Adverse yaw and rudder with aileron while the bank is changing

texts.0: SP, due to aileron applied without simultaneous rudder in the same direction, left adverse yaw uncountered so the nose yawed opposite the direction of the roll on both entry and rollout. The ball stayed deflected, heading error exceeded 10 degrees and the aircraft was flying out of balance when the IP intervened on the controls. SP never crosschecked the turn and slip indicator.
texts.1: SP, due to rudder pressure applied late and not held for as long as the bank was changing, allowed the nose to yaw away from the direction of aileron input. Heading error reached about 10 degrees, at the limit of the standard, and coordination improved only after repeated IP prompting to step on the ball. No IP control input was needed.
texts.2: SP, due to rudder used on entry but released during the rollout, left the aileron drag effect uncountered as the wings came level and finished roughly 7 degrees off the assigned heading, between the 5 and 10 degree limits. SP saw the ball out, stepped on it and corrected the heading in good time without prompting.
texts.3: SP applied rudder pressure simultaneously with aileron and in the same direction, and held it as long as the bank was changing on both entry and rollout. The ball was crosschecked and kept centered and headings were held within 5 degrees. The rudder pressure was matched to the airspeed and the amount of aileron deflection.
texts.4: SP countered adverse yaw exactly, with rudder proportioned to airspeed and aileron deflection, so the ball did not leave the center during any roll in or out. Headings were captured with negligible error and the nose never yawed opposite the direction of the roll. Coordination was maintained without any visible reference to the instrument.
texts.marginal: SP countered adverse yaw and stayed within standards, but the ball moved slightly off center at the start of each roll before the rudder was added. The trend was rudder applied just after the aileron rather than with it. SP is expected to apply both pressures simultaneously and to hold rudder while the bank is changing.

texts_at.1: SP had coordination corrected only after repeated IP prompting to step on the ball, reaching a heading error of about 10 degrees, at the limit of the standard, because rudder pressure had been applied late and not held for as long as the bank was changing. No IP control input was needed. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to hold rudder for the whole bank change without needing the prompt to step on the ball.

This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to hold the rudder through the rollout rather than releasing it early.
texts_at.3: SP applied rudder pressure simultaneously with aileron and in the same direction, holding it as long as the bank was changing on both entry and rollout, crosschecking the ball to keep it centered and holding headings within 5 degrees with the rudder pressure matched to airspeed and aileron deflection. One rollout carried the ball slightly off center for a moment before it centered. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to hold the ball centered through every rollout, not just most of them.

texts_above.2: SP saw the ball out and stepped on it, correcting the heading in good time without prompting, finishing roughly 7 degrees off the assigned heading, between the 5 and 10 degree limits, after rudder released during the rollout had briefly left the aileron drag effect uncountered. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good adverse-yaw and rudder coordination.

Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed adverse-yaw and rudder coordination.
texts_above.4: SP countered adverse yaw exactly, with rudder proportioned to airspeed and aileron deflection so the ball did not leave center during any roll in or out, capturing headings with negligible error and maintaining coordination without any visible reference to the instrument. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional adverse-yaw and rudder coordination.

error_modes.label: Skid and slip from bank angle versus turn rate

texts.0: SP, due to excessive bottom rudder in relation to the bank angle, held the aircraft in a sustained skid through the turns and did not correct the mismatch between bank and turn rate. The flight path departed from a true circle, heading errors exceeded 10 degrees and the IP intervened on the controls because of the roll risk from a skid at slow airspeed. SP did not read the turn and slip indicator.
texts.1: SP, due to insufficient bottom rudder in relation to the aileron pressure, flew the established turns in a slip with too much bank angle for the turn rate. Heading and altitude were driven to about 10 degrees and 300 ft, at the limits of the standards, and were corrected only after IP prompting. Control of the aircraft was retained without IP control input.
texts.2: SP, due to rudder pressure held after the bank was set, produced a mild skid that opened the turn and left roughly 7 degrees of heading error, between the 5 and 10 degree limits. SP identified the ball displacement, matched the bank to the turn rate and returned to coordinated flight in good time without prompting.
texts.3: SP kept bank angle matched to turn rate so the flight path stayed a true circle, with no skid or slip in the level turns and no rudder-only turning tendency in level flight. Headings were held within 5 degrees and altitude within 150 ft, with the ball centered throughout.
texts.4: SP flew every turn coordinated, with bank and turn rate matched from entry to rollout and the ball effectively motionless in the center. No variation of the circular flight path from uncoordinated control, erratic bank or airspeed change appeared. Heading and altitude deviations were negligible.
texts.marginal: SP flew coordinated turns within standards, but a small amount of bottom rudder was carried into the established turn. The trend was a slight skid that SP removed only when the ball came into the scan. SP is expected to neutralize the rudder once the bank is set and to keep the ball in the crosscheck.

texts_at.1: SP had the aircraft corrected only after IP prompting, with heading and altitude driven to about 10 degrees and 300 ft, at the limits of the standards, because bottom rudder had been insufficient in relation to the aileron pressure and the turns had been flown in a slip. Control of the aircraft was retained once the prompting had been given. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to match rudder to aileron pressure from the start of the turn without needing it prompted.

This is consistent with the expected proficiency for the Training Section. SP is expected to release the rudder as soon as the bank is set so the skid does not develop.
texts_at.3: SP kept bank angle matched to turn rate so the flight path stayed a true circle, with no skid or slip in level turns and no rudder-only turning tendency in level flight, holding headings within 5 degrees and altitude within 150 ft with the ball centered throughout. One turn carried a trace of skid before it was removed. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to keep every turn as clean as the best one.

texts_above.2: SP identified the ball displacement and matched the bank to the turn rate, returning to coordinated flight in good time without prompting, leaving roughly 7 degrees of heading error, between the 5 and 10 degree limits, after rudder held after the bank was set had produced a mild skid. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid skid and slip control against turn rate.
texts_above.3: SP kept bank angle matched to turn rate on every turn so the flight path stayed a true circle, with no skid or slip in level turns and no rudder-only turning tendency, holding headings within 5 degrees and altitude within 150 ft with the ball centered throughout the sortie. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate skid and slip control against turn rate.
texts_above.4: SP flew every turn coordinated, with bank and turn rate matched from entry to rollout and the ball effectively motionless in the center, with no variation of the circular flight path from uncoordinated control and heading and altitude deviations negligible throughout. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary skid and slip control against turn rate.

error_modes.label: Slipstream effect and rudder matched to PCL movement

texts.0: SP, due to no rudder input matched to the amount and rate of PCL movement, let the corkscrew slipstream yaw the nose left on every power increase and right on every reduction. Heading swung beyond 10 degrees uncorrected and the aircraft stayed uncoordinated until the IP intervened on the controls. SP did not connect the yaw with the power handling.
texts.1: SP, due to right rudder applied only after the nose had already swung on the power increase, allowed heading error of about 10 degrees, at the limit of the standard. The rudder was coordinated with the PCL only after repeated IP prompting, and the heading was regained slowly. No IP input on the controls was required.
texts.2: SP, due to rudder pressure not proportioned to a rapid PCL movement, applied too much rudder and swung the nose right by roughly 7 degrees, between the 5 and 10 degree limits. SP saw the nose moving against the reference on the horizon, eased the rudder and steadied the heading in good time without prompting.
texts.3: SP moved the right foot forward as the PCL went forward and applied left rudder on power reductions, so the slipstream-induced yaw was countered as it developed. Heading was held within 5 degrees through all power changes and the ball stayed centered. The amount of rudder was matched to the amount and rate of PCL movement.
texts.4: SP countered the slipstream effect with rudder applied simultaneously with every power change, so the nose did not move against the horizon reference at all. Heading remained effectively constant through large power changes in both directions. Coordination during power handling was continuous and required no comment.
texts.marginal: SP countered the slipstream yaw and held heading within standards, but the rudder went in a moment after the power rather than with it. The trend was a small left swing on each power increase that SP then removed. SP is expected to move the right foot with the PCL so the yaw never develops.

texts_at.1: SP had the heading regained slowly, only after repeated IP prompting, with heading error of about 10 degrees, at the limit of the standard, because no rudder input had been matched to the amount and rate of PCL movement. No IP input on the controls was required. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to match rudder to the power movement without needing it prompted.
